newLocations.description: A large inn located near the Bristol docks where the Squire is staying.

items.text: Will we be able to see the ship before we sail, sir?
I look around the inn to see if Dr. Livesey is there.
I follow Trelawney into the inn.

story_entries.content: I carry the squire's note to the Spy-glass tavern and hang at the door, afraid to go in.

“Sail!” says he. “We sail tomorrow!”

When I had done breakfasting the squire gave me a note addressed to John Silver, at the sign of the Spy-glass, and told me I should easily find the place by following the line of the docks and keeping a bright lookout for a little tavern with a large brass telescope for sign. I set off, overjoyed at this opportunity to see some more of the ships and seamen, and picked my way among a great crowd of people and carts and bales, for the dock was now at its busiest, until I found the tavern in question.

It was a bright enough little place of entertainment. The sign was newly painted; the windows had neat red curtains; the floor was cleanly sanded. There was a street on each side and an open door on both, which made the large, low room pretty clear to see in, in spite of clouds of tobacco smoke.

The customers were mostly seafaring men, and they talked so loudly that I hung at the door, almost afraid to enter.

As I was waiting, a man came out of a side room, and at a glance I was sure he must be Long John. His left leg was cut off close by the hip, and under the left shoulder he carried a crutch, which he managed with wonderful dexterity, hopping about upon it like a bird. He was very tall and strong, with a face as big as a ham--plain and pale, but intelligent and smiling. Indeed, he seemed in the most cheerful spirits, whistling as he moved about among the tables, with a merry word or a slap on the shoulder for the more favoured of his guests.

metadata.summary: Jim Hawkins reaches the Spy-glass tavern and observes Long John Silver emerging from a side room.

items.text: I step inside the tavern to find the man.
"Excuse me, sir," I say, approaching him, "I have a message for you from Squire Trelawney."
I study the man's face and his nimble way of walking with his crutch.

story_entries.content: I walk right up to the man and hold out the note, asking, "Mr. Silver, sir?"

Now, to tell you the truth, from the very first mention of Long John in Squire Trelawney’s letter I had taken a fear in my mind that he might prove to be the very one-legged sailor whom I had watched for so long at the old Benbow. But one look at the man before me was enough. I had seen the captain, and Black Dog, and the blind man, Pew, and I thought I knew what a buccaneer was like--a very different creature, according to me, from this clean and pleasant-tempered landlord.

I plucked up courage at once, crossed the threshold, and walked right up to the man where he stood, propped on his crutch, talking to a customer.

“Mr. Silver, sir?” I asked, holding out the note.

“Yes, my lad,” said he; “such is my name, to be sure. And who may you be?” And then as he saw the squire’s letter, he seemed to me to give something almost like a start.

“Oh!” said he, quite loud, and offering his hand. “I see. You are our new cabin-boy; pleased I am to see you.”

And he took my hand in his large firm grasp.

Just then one of the customers at the far side rose suddenly and made for the door. It was close by him, and he was out in the street in a moment. But his hurry had attracted my notice, and I recognized him at glance. It was the tallow-faced man, wanting two fingers, who had come first to the Admiral Benbow.

“Oh,” I cried, “stop him! It’s Black Dog!”

metadata.summary: Jim Hawkins meets Long John Silver at the Spy-glass tavern and realizes that the man who just fled is Black Dog.

items.text: I dash out of the tavern to chase after the fleeing man.
I exclaim to Silver, 'Sir, that man—he's Black Dog!'
I step out onto the street to get a better look at the crowd.

story_entries.content: "Dog, sir," I say. "Has Mr. Trelawney not told you of the buccaneers? He was one of them."

“I don’t care two coppers who he is,” cried Silver. “But he hasn’t paid his score. Harry, run and catch him.”

One of the others who was nearest the door leaped up and started in pursuit.

“If he were Admiral Hawke he shall pay his score,” cried Silver; and then, relinquishing my hand, “Who did you say he was?” he asked. “Black what?”

“Dog, sir,” said I. “Has Mr. Trelawney not told you of the buccaneers? He was one of them.”

“So?” cried Silver. “In my house! Ben, run and help Harry. One of those swabs, was he? Was that you drinking with him, Morgan? Step up here.”

The man whom he called Morgan--an old, grey-haired, mahogany-faced sailor--came forward pretty sheepishly, rolling his quid.

“Now, Morgan,” said Long John very sternly, “you never clapped your eyes on that Black--Black Dog before, did you, now?”

“Not I, sir,” said Morgan with a salute.

“You didn’t know his name, did you?”

“No, sir.”

“By the powers, Tom Morgan, it’s as good for you!” exclaimed the landlord. “If you had been mixed up with the like of that, you would never have put another foot in my house, you may lay to that. And what was he saying to you?”

“I don’t rightly know, sir,” answered Morgan.

“Do you call that a head on your shoulders, or a blessed dead-eye?” cried Long John. “Don’t rightly know, don’t you! Perhaps you don’t happen to rightly know who you was speaking to, perhaps? Come, now, what was he jawing--v’yages, cap’ns, ships? Pipe up! What was it?”

metadata.summary: Jim identifies Black Dog as a buccaneer, prompting Silver to order a pursuit and sternly interrogate Morgan about his connection to the fleeing man.

items.text: "Are you sure he isn't dangerous, sir?" I ask, my voice trembling slightly.
I watch Morgan closely, trying to see if he's hiding something behind his sheepish salute.
I step back to give Silver room as he confronts Morgan.

story_entries.content: "That he did, you may be sure," I say. "I knew that blind man too. His name was Pew."

“We was a-talkin’ of keel-hauling,” answered Morgan.

“Keel-hauling, was you? And a mighty suitable thing, too, and you may lay to that. Get back to your place for a lubber, Tom.”

And then, as Morgan rolled back to his seat, Silver added to me in a confidential whisper that was very flattering, as I thought, “He’s quite an honest man, Tom Morgan, on’y stupid. And now,” he ran on again, aloud, “let’s see--Black Dog? No, I don’t know the name, not I. Yet I kind of think I’ve--yes, I’ve seen the swab. He used to come here with a blind beggar, he used.”

“That he did, you may be sure,” said I. “I knew that blind man too. His name was Pew.”

“It was!” cried Silver, now quite excited. “Pew! That were his name for certain. Ah, he looked a shark, he did! If we run down this Black Dog, now, there’ll be news for Cap’n Trelawney! Ben’s a good runner; few seamen run better than Ben. He should run him down, hand over hand, by the powers! He talked o’ keel-hauling, did he? I’LL keel-haul him!”

All the time he was jerking out these phrases he was stumping up and down the tavern on his crutch, slapping tables with his hand, and giving such a show of excitement as would have convinced an Old Bailey judge or a Bow Street runner. My suspicions had been thoroughly reawakened on finding Black Dog at the Spy-glass, and I watched the cook narrowly. But he was too deep, and too ready, and too clever for me, and by the time the two men had come back out of breath and confessed that they had lost the track in a crowd, and been scolded like thieves, I would have gone bail for the innocence of Long John Silver.

metadata.summary: Jim identifies the blind man as Pew, triggering a theatrical and highly animated reaction from Long John Silver.

items.text: "What do you know about this Pew, Mr. Silver?" I ask, watching him closely.
I study Silver's face to see if his sudden excitement is genuine.
I move toward the bar to get a closer look at the men who just returned.

story_entries.content: I listen to Silver, and join in his laughter.

“See here, now, Hawkins,” said he, “here’s a blessed hard thing on a man like me, now, ain’t it? There’s Cap’n Trelawney--what’s he to think? Here I have this confounded son of a Dutchman sitting in my own house drinking of my own rum! Here you comes and tells me of it plain; and here I let him give us all the slip before my blessed deadlights! Now, Hawkins, you do me justice with the cap’n. You’re a lad, you are, but you’re as smart as paint. I see that when you first come in. Now, here it is: What could I do, with this old timber I hobble on? When I was an A B master mariner I’d have come up alongside of him, hand over hand, and broached him to in a brace of old shakes, I would; but now--”

And then, all of a sudden, he stopped, and his jaw dropped as though he had remembered something.

“The score!” he burst out. “Three goes o’ rum! Why, shiver my timbers, if I hadn’t forgotten my score!”

And falling on a bench, he laughed until the tears ran down his cheeks. I could not help joining, and we laughed together, peal after peal, until the tavern rang again.

metadata.summary: Jim joins in Long John Silver's boisterous laughter after the cook remembers his forgotten rum score.

items.text: I reach out and pat his arm as the laughter subsides.
I say, 'You'll have to settle that debt with the landlord then, Mr. Silver!'
I watch him through the laughter, searching for any sign that his outburst is a calculated performance.

story_entries.content: I join his laughter, then walk with him along the quays to the inn.

“Why, what a precious old sea-calf I am!” he said at last, wiping his cheeks. “You and me should get on well, Hawkins, for I’ll take my davy I should be rated ship’s boy. But come now, stand by to go about. This won’t do. Dooty is dooty, messmates. I’ll put on my old cockerel hat, and step along of you to Cap’n Trelawney, and report this here affair. For mind you, it’s serious, young Hawkins; and neither you nor me’s come out of it with what I should make so bold as to call credit. Nor you neither, says you; not smart--none of the pair of us smart. But dash my buttons! That was a good un about my score.”

And he began to laugh again, and that so heartily, that though I did not see the joke as he did, I was again obliged to join him in his mirth.

On our little walk along the quays, he made himself the most interesting companion, telling me about the different ships that we passed by, their rig, tonnage, and nationality, explaining the work that was going forward--how one was discharging, another taking in cargo, and a third making ready for sea--and every now and then telling me some little anecdote of ships or seamen or repeating a nautical phrase till I had learned it perfectly. I began to see that here was one of the best of possible shipmates.

When we got to the inn, the squire and Dr. Livesey were seated together, finishing a quart of ale with a toast in it, before they should go aboard the schooner on a visit of inspection.

metadata.summary: Jim walks with Long John Silver along the quays to Trelawney's Inn, where he finds Squire Trelawney and Dr. Livesey.

items.text: "What is it you were discussing?" I ask as we approach the table.
I take a seat at the table alongside Silver and the others.
I watch the expression on Dr. Livesey's face as we arrive.

story_entries.content: I bear out what Long John says, then go aboard the Hispaniola with the squire and the doctor.

Long John told the story from first to last, with a great deal of spirit and the most perfect truth. “That was how it were, now, weren’t it, Hawkins?” he would say, now and again, and I could always bear him entirely out.

The two gentlemen regretted that Black Dog had got away, but we all agreed there was nothing to be done, and after he had been complimented, Long John took up his crutch and departed.

“All hands aboard by four this afternoon,” shouted the squire after him.

“Aye, aye, sir,” cried the cook, in the passage.

“Well, squire,” said Dr. Livesey, “I don’t put much faith in your discoveries, as a general thing; but I will say this, John Silver suits me.”

“The man’s a perfect trump,” declared the squire.

“And now,” added the doctor, “Jim may come on board with us, may he not?”

“To be sure he may,” says squire. “Take your hat, Hawkins, and we’ll see the ship.”

The Hispaniola lay some way out, and we went under the figureheads and round the sterns of many other ships, and their cables sometimes grated underneath our keel, and sometimes swung above us. At last, however, we got alongside, and were met and saluted as we stepped aboard by the mate, Mr. Arrow, a brown old sailor with earrings in his ears and a squint. He and the squire were very thick and friendly, but I soon observed that things were not the same between Mr. Trelawney and the captain.

metadata.summary: Jim, Dr. Livesey, and Squire Trelawney board the Hispaniola, where they are greeted by Mr. Arrow, and Jim observes a tension between Trelawney and the captain.

newLocations.description: A large schooner intended for the voyage to find Flint's treasure.

items.text: I examine the other sailors standing on the deck.
I walk toward the stern to see the captain.
“Who is the captain, sir?” I ask Mr. Arrow.

story_entries.content: I go down into the cabin with the squire and the doctor.

This last was a sharp-looking man who seemed angry with everything on board and was soon to tell us why, for we had hardly got down into the cabin when a sailor followed us.

“Captain Smollett, sir, axing to speak with you,” said he.

“I am always at the captain’s orders. Show him in,” said the squire.

The captain, who was close behind his messenger, entered at once and shut the door behind him.

“Well, Captain Smollett, what have you to say? All well, I hope; all shipshape and seaworthy?”

“Well, sir,” said the captain, “better speak plain, I believe, even at the risk of offence. I don’t like this cruise; I don’t like the men; and I don’t like my officer. That’s short and sweet.”

“Perhaps, sir, you don’t like the ship?” inquired the squire, very angry, as I could see.

“I can’t speak as to that, sir, not having seen her tried,” said the captain. “She seems a clever craft; more I can’t say.”

“Possibly, sir, you may not like your employer, either?” says the squire.

But here Dr. Livesey cut in.

“Stay a bit,” said he, “stay a bit. No use of such questions as that but to produce ill feeling. The captain has said too much or he has said too little, and I’m bound to say that I require an explanation of his words. You don’t, you say, like this cruise. Now, why?”

metadata.summary: Jim, the Squire, and the Doctor enter the cabin, where Captain Smollett expresses his dissatisfaction with the cruise, the crew, and the officer.

droppedRefs.detail: Unrecognized or malformed placeholder: Captain Smollett

items.text: I say, 'Please, Captain, tell us more about these concerns.'
I watch Captain Smollett to see how he reacts to Dr. Livesey's intervention.
I take a step back to give the men more space to talk.

story_entries.content: I listen.

“I was engaged, sir, on what we call sealed orders, to sail this ship for that gentleman where he should bid me,” said the captain. “So far so good. But now I find that every man before the mast knows more than I do. I don’t call that fair, now, do you?”

“No,” said Dr. Livesey, “I don’t.”

“Next,” said the captain, “I learn we are going after treasure--hear it from my own hands, mind you. Now, treasure is ticklish work; I don’t like treasure voyages on any account, and I don’t like them, above all, when they are secret and when (begging your pardon, Mr. Trelawney) the secret has been told to the parrot.”

“Silver’s parrot?” asked the squire.

“It’s a way of speaking,” said the captain. “Blabbed, I mean. It’s my belief neither of you gentlemen know what you are about, but I’ll tell you my way of it--life or death, and a close run.”

“That is all clear, and, I dare say, true enough,” replied Dr. Livesey. “We take the risk, but we are not so ignorant as you believe us. Next, you say you don’t like the crew. Are they not good seamen?”

“I don’t like them, sir,” returned Captain Smollett. “And I think I should have had the choosing of my own hands, if you go to that.”

“Perhaps you should,” replied the doctor. “My friend should, perhaps, have taken you along with him; but the slight, if there be one, was unintentional. And you don’t like Mr. Arrow?”

metadata.summary: Captain Smollett expresses his dissatisfaction to Dr. Livesey and Trelawney regarding the secrecy of the voyage and the lack of command over his crew and officers.

items.text: I shift in my chair, feeling the tension in the cabin rising.
"Is there anything we can do to make the voyage safer, Captain?" I ask.
I study Captain Smollett's expression to see if he is truly concerned.

story_entries.content: I keep listening.

“I don’t, sir. I believe he’s a good seaman, but he’s too free with the crew to be a good officer. A mate should keep himself to himself--shouldn’t drink with the men before the mast!”

“Do you mean he drinks?” cried the squire.

“No, sir,” replied the captain, “only that he’s too familiar.”

“Well, now, and the short and long of it, captain?” asked the doctor. “Tell us what you want.”

“Well, gentlemen, are you determined to go on this cruise?”

“Like iron,” answered the squire.

“Very good,” said the captain. “Then, as you’ve heard me very patiently, saying things that I could not prove, hear me a few words more. They are putting the powder and the arms in the fore hold. Now, you have a good place under the cabin; why not put them there?--first point. Then, you are bringing four of your own people with you, and they tell me some of them are to be berthed forward. Why not give them the berths here beside the cabin?--second point.”

“Any more?” asked Mr. Trelawney.

“One more,” said the captain. “There’s been too much blabbing already.”

“Far too much,” agreed the doctor.

“I’ll tell you what I’ve heard myself,” continued Captain Smollett: “that you have a map of an island, that there’s crosses on the map to show where treasure is, and that the island lies--” And then he named the latitude and longitude exactly.

“I never told that,” cried the squire, “to a soul!”

“The hands know it, sir,” returned the captain.

metadata.summary: Captain Smollett advises on ship security and secrecy, expressing concerns about the crew's knowledge of the treasure map and the influence of officers like Mr. Arrow.

items.text: "Do you believe the crew is already planning something against us?"
I observe the tension on the Captain's face as he finishes speaking.
I nod silently, absorbing the gravity of the Captain's warnings.

story_entries.content: I keep listening to the captain.

“Livesey, that must have been you or Hawkins,” cried the squire.

“It doesn’t much matter who it was,” replied the doctor. And I could see that neither he nor the captain paid much regard to Mr. Trelawney’s protestations. Neither did I, to be sure, he was so loose a talker; yet in this case I believe he was really right and that nobody had told the situation of the island.

“Well, gentlemen,” continued the captain, “I don’t know who has this map; but I make it a point, it shall be kept secret even from me and Mr. Arrow. Otherwise I would ask you to let me resign.”

“I see,” said the doctor. “You wish us to keep this matter dark and to make a garrison of the stern part of the ship, manned with my friend’s own people, and provided with all the arms and powder on board. In other words, you fear a mutiny.”

“Sir,” said Captain Smollett, “with no intention to take offence, I deny your right to put words into my mouth. No captain, sir, would be justified in going to sea at all if he had ground enough to say that. As for Mr. Arrow, I believe him thoroughly honest; some of the men are the same; all may be for what I know. But I am responsible for the ship’s safety and the life of every man Jack aboard of her. I see things going, as I think, not quite right. And I ask you to take certain precautions or let me resign my berth. And that’s all.”

metadata.summary: Captain Smollett details his concerns regarding the crew and the map, proposing measures to prevent potential mutiny.

items.text: "Are you saying we should be afraid of the men, sir?" I ask.
I watch the Captain's eyes, looking for any sign of doubt or fear.
I shift my weight, feeling the sudden tension in the cabin.

story_entries.content: I listen to the conversation and then follow them out onto the deck.

“Captain Smollett,” began the doctor with a smile, “did ever you hear the fable of the mountain and the mouse? You’ll excuse me, I dare say, but you remind me of that fable. When you came in here, I’ll stake my wig, you meant more than this.”

“Doctor,” said the captain, “you are smart. When I came in here I meant to get discharged. I had no thought that Mr. Trelawney would hear a word.”

“No more I would,” cried the squire. “Had Livesey not been here I should have seen you to the deuce. As it is, I have heard you. I will do as you desire, but I think the worse of you.”

“That’s as you please, sir,” said the captain. “You’ll find I do my duty.”

And with that he took his leave.

“Trelawney,” said the doctor, “contrary to all my notions, I believed you have managed to get two honest men on board with you--that man and John Silver.”

“Silver, if you like,” cried the squire; “but as for that intolerable humbug, I declare I think his conduct unmanly, unsailorly, and downright un-English.”

“Well,” says the doctor, “we shall see.”

When we came on deck, the men had begun already to take out the arms and powder, yo-ho-ing at their work, while the captain and Mr. Arrow stood by superintending.

metadata.summary: Jim joins the others on the deck of the Hispaniola, where the crew is moving arms and powder under the supervision of Captain Smollett and Arrow.

items.text: I walk towards the crew to get a closer look at the arms and powder.
I observe the sailors as they work, looking for any signs of discontent.
“Will the crew be satisfied with these new arrangements, Captain?” I ask.

story_entries.content: I help change the powder and the berths.

The new arrangement was quite to my liking. The whole schooner had been overhauled; six berths had been made astern out of what had been the after-part of the main hold; and this set of cabins was only joined to the galley and forecastle by a sparred passage on the port side. It had been originally meant that the captain, Mr. Arrow, Hunter, Joyce, the doctor, and the squire were to occupy these six berths. Now Redruth and I were to get two of them and Mr. Arrow and the captain were to sleep on deck in the companion, which had been enlarged on each side till you might almost have called it a round-house. Very low it was still, of course; but there was room to swing two hammocks, and even the mate seemed pleased with the arrangement. Even he, perhaps, had been doubtful as to the crew, but that is only guess, for as you shall hear, we had not long the benefit of his opinion.

We were all hard at work, changing the powder and the berths, when the last man or two, and Long John along with them, came off in a shore-boat.

The cook came up the side like a monkey for cleverness, and as soon as he saw what was doing, “So ho, mates!” says he. “What’s this?”

“We’re a-changing of the powder, Jack,” answers one.

“Why, by the powers,” cried Long John, “if we do, we’ll miss the morning tide!”

“My orders!” said the captain shortly. “You may go below, my man. Hands will want supper.”

metadata.summary: Jim helps reorganize the Hispaniola's berths and powder when Long John Silver arrives in a shore-boat and is dismissed by the Captain.

items.text: I drop my work and rush to help the men pull the boat alongside.
“Good morning, Mr. Silver!” I call out to him.
I watch Silver closely as he climbs up the side of the ship.

story_entries.content: I examine the long brass swivel amidships, and hurry off to the cook for work.

“Aye, aye, sir,” answered the cook, and touching his forelock, he disappeared at once in the direction of his galley.

“That’s a good man, captain,” said the doctor.

“Very likely, sir,” replied Captain Smollett. “Easy with that, men--easy,” he ran on, to the fellows who were shifting the powder; and then suddenly observing me examining the swivel we carried amidships, a long brass nine, “Here you, ship’s boy,” he cried, “out o’ that! Off with you to the cook and get some work.”

And then as I was hurrying off I heard him say, quite loudly, to the doctor, “I’ll have no favourites on my ship.”

I assure you I was quite of the squire’s way of thinking, and hated the captain deeply.

metadata.summary: Captain Smollett reprimands Jim for idling at the brass swivel and orders him to go work for the cook.

items.text: I hurry toward the galley to find the cook.
"Yes, sir!" I call back to the Captain as I turn away.
I look back at the Captain and the Doctor to see if they are still watching me.

chapters.title: The Admiral Benbow and the Treasure Map

After you and your mother escape a pirate raid, you deliver a treasure map found in the captain's chest to Squire Trelawney and Dr. Livesey. As they fit out the Hispaniola with Long John Silver as cook, you join them on board where Captain Smollett expresses serious concerns regarding the voyage.

happenings.title: Dr. Livesey's visit
happenings.description: Dr. Livesey arrived to visit Jim's ailing father, had a bit of dinner from Jim's mother, and went into the parlour to smoke a pipe, where the captain was sitting and singing.

happenings.title: The meeting with Captain Smollett
happenings.description: Captain Smollett meets with Jim, Dr. Livesey, and Squire Trelawney in the cabin to express his dissatisfaction with the voyage, the crew, and his officer, Arrow. He requests that the powder and arms be moved to the fore hold and that Trelawney's men be berthed near the cabin. He also reveals that he has learned the precise location of the treasure map.

happenings.title: The encounter at the Spy-glass
happenings.description: Jim Hawkins approaches Long John Silver at the Spy-glass with Squire Trelawney's note. Upon seeing Black Dog flee the tavern, Silver orders a pursuit and interrogates Tom Morgan about his connection to the fugitive. The pursuit fails, and the runners, Ben and Harry, are scolded by Silver for losing the trail.

happenings.title: The arrival of the stranger
happenings.description: A pale, tallowy man with two fingers missing on his left hand enters the parlour, asks Jim for rum, and then beckons him to come closer.

happenings.title: Searching the Captain's belongings
happenings.description: After finding a black spot near the Captain's body, Jim and his mother find the key to his chest hanging around his neck. They open the chest to find various items, including clothes, silver, a watch, and a bag of gold.

happenings.title: Silver's laughter and walk to the inn
happenings.description: Silver suddenly remembers he owes a score of rum, leading to a bout of laughter with Jim; they then walk together from the quays to the inn.

happenings.title: Return to the Admiral Benbow
happenings.description: Jim and Mr. Dance return to the Admiral Benbow to find the house in a state of smash; Jim informs Dance that he has the object the men were seeking in his breast pocket.

happenings.title: The encounter between Black Dog and the Captain
happenings.description: The stranger, who identifies himself as Black Dog, approaches the Admiral Benbow to find his mate Bill. After interacting with Jim Hawkins, Black Dog and Jim hide behind a door in the parlour to surprise the captain. When the captain arrives, Black Dog reveals himself, causing the captain to appear deathly ill with shock.

happenings.title: Rearranging the Hispaniola
happenings.description: Jim and the crew work to change the powder and rearrange the berths on the ship. Long John Silver arrives via a shore-boat and notes that the work might cause them to miss the morning tide.

happenings.title: The journey to Bristol
happenings.description: Jim and Redruth traveled by mail coach from the Royal George on the heath, arriving in Bristol at dawn.

happenings.title: The voyage discussion
happenings.description: Trelawney announces plans to sail in ten days with the Hispaniola and a fine crew, intending for Jim to serve as cabin-boy. Dr. Livesey agrees to join the voyage and will bail for Jim, and both agree to keep the matter of the treasure secret.

happenings.title: The escape of the lugger
happenings.description: At Kitt's Hole, the lugger is seen fleeing; after a voice warns Supervisor Dance to stay out of the moonlight, a shot is fired and the vessel disappears.

happenings.title: The restoration of the Admiral Benbow
happenings.description: Trelawney had the Admiral Benbow repaired and repainted, added new furniture including a beautiful armchair for Jim's mother in the bar, and found her an apprentice boy.

happenings.title: The meeting in the Captain's cabin
happenings.description: Captain Smollett expresses his concern regarding the secrecy of the map and the potential for mutiny. Dr. Livesey suggests establishing a garrison in the stern to ensure safety, a precaution the Captain agrees to support through specific precautions.

happenings.title: The flight of the buccaneers and the death of Pew
happenings.description: Following a signal from the hillside, the buccaneers scatter in all directions. Pew, left behind and calling for his comrades, is trampled and killed by riders on horseback.

happenings.title: The death of Jim's father
happenings.description: Jim's father dies suddenly in the evening.

happenings.title: The approach of the blind man
happenings.description: While counting the gold, Jim and his mother hear the blind man's stick tapping on the road. The man attempts to enter the inn, but after a period of silence, the tapping fades away, followed by a low whistle from the hill.

happenings.title: The recruitment of the crew
happenings.description: Trelawney met Long John Silver, an old sailor looking for work as a cook, on the dock. Silver helped assemble a company of tough old sailors, and Arrow was appointed as sailing master.

happenings.title: The arrival of the revenue officers
happenings.description: Revenue officers, including a lad from the hamlet and Supervisor Dance, arrive at the roadside, responding to the accident involving Jim and his mother.

happenings.title: Meeting Squire Trelawney at the inn
happenings.description: Jim and Redruth met Squire Trelawney at his inn, where he mentioned that Dr. Livesey had arrived from London and the ship's company was complete.

happenings.title: The visit to the Hispaniola
happenings.description: Silver recounts his story to the group. After Silver departs, Squire Trelawney, Dr. Livesey, and Jim board the Hispaniola, where they are met by the mate, Mr. Arrow.

happenings.title: Arrival at Dr. Livesey's house
happenings.description: Jim, Mr. Dance, and Dogger arrive at Dr. Livesey's house and are admitted into the library, where the doctor is dining with the squire.

happenings.title: The Captain's request
happenings.description: The seaman promises Jim a monthly payment of fourpence to keep a lookout for a seafaring man with one leg.

happenings.title: Smollett's command to Jim
happenings.description: While men shift powder on the deck, Captain Smollett observes Jim examining a brass swivel and orders him to the cook for work. He also informs Dr. Livesey that he will have no favourites on his ship.

happenings.title: The encounter with the blind beggar
happenings.description: A blind, deformed figure arrives at the Admiral Benbow, threatens Jim Hawkins, and forces his way into the parlour to meet Billy Bones. He passes a mysterious object into the Captain's hand, after which he flees, causing the Captain to collapse and die of apoplexy.

happenings.title: The flight of Jim and his mother
happenings.description: Jim and his mother flee the Admiral Benbow and take shelter under the arch of the bridge underpass.

happenings.title: Seeking help in the hamlet
happenings.description: Jim and his mother travel to the nearby hamlet to seek assistance. The villagers, terrified by the reputation of Captain Flint, refuse to help defend the Admiral Benbow, though some agree to ride to Dr. Livesey's. Jim's mother delivers a defiant speech, vowing to return to the inn to claim their money.

happenings.title: The discussion on the deck
happenings.description: On the deck, Captain Smollett asserts his intent to do his duty despite Trelawney's disapproval. Dr. Livesey notes that Smollett and Long John Silver appear to be the only honest men on board.

happenings.title: The meeting at Dr. Livesey's
happenings.description: Dr. Livesey, the Squire, Supervisor Dance, and Jim Hawkins meet at the doctor's house to discuss the recent events at the Admiral Benbow and the contents of an oilskin packet. The Squire expresses a desire to hunt for Captain Flint's treasure, and the doctor prepares to open the packet, which contains a book and a sealed paper.

happenings.title: Sighting Long John Silver at the Spy-glass
happenings.description: After delivering the Squire's note to the Spy-glass tavern, Jim encountered Long John Silver, a tall and strong man with a missing leg who moved with a crutch.

happenings.title: The arrival of the seaman
happenings.description: A tall, strong, heavy, nut-brown man with a sabre cut on his cheek arrives at the Admiral Benbow with a sea-chest on a hand-barrow. He asks for a glass of rum and settles in at the inn.

happenings.title: The reading of the squire's letter
happenings.description: Jim reads a letter from Trelawney to Redruth. The letter reveals that the Hispaniola has been purchased through Blandly and mentions the mission's focus on treasure.

happenings.title: The confrontation between the captain and Dr. Livesey
happenings.description: After Dr. Livesey's singing irritates the captain, the captain threatens the doctor with a sailor's clasp-knife. The doctor remains calm and threatens the captain with legal action, causing the captain to yield.

happenings.title: The raid on the Admiral Benbow
happenings.description: Pew and his men rush the Admiral Benbow, discovering the chest has been emptied and Billy Bones is dead. Pew orders his men to search the house and find the escapees.

happenings.title: Dr. Livesey's medical intervention
happenings.description: Dr. Livesey arrived to treat the Captain, who was suffering from a stroke. He examined the Captain's tattooed arm and performed bloodletting with a lancet. The Captain briefly regained consciousness to ask about Black Dog.

happenings.title: The return to the Admiral Benbow
happenings.description: Jim and his mother return to the Admiral Benbow under the cover of a foggy, moonlit night. They enter the parlour, where they find the Captain's body lying on the floor, and discuss the need to retrieve a key.

happenings.title: Billy Bones's warning
happenings.description: Billy Bones warns Jim that if he receives the black spot, Jim should inform Dr. Livesey to summon the authorities and Flint's old crew. He also warns Jim to watch for a seafaring man with one leg.
